title: Netflix & Paramount’s WBD Fight Heats Up + Oracle Falls as AI Doubts Grow | The Weekly Wrap
summary: Eisman contrasts Oracle’s accelerating AI backlog with its funding deficit, favors Paramount in the Warner Bros. bidding contest, and worries about a possible break in AI model scaling. He remains invested in AI and declines to make a broad bearish call. A viewer describes concrete coding-productivity gains, which Eisman considers insufficient by themselves to justify total infrastructure spending. Oracle’s cash-flow statements validate the funding concern, and Paramount displaced Netflix. The latter outcome does not prove Eisman’s antitrust or political explanation. His claim that almost all GDP growth comes from AI remains inadequately established.
assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
speaker_map_notes: Eisman narrates the wrap and explicitly reads an edited viewer email from Sebastian. Claims in that email remain attributed to the viewer; Eisman separately comments on aggregate ROI.
framework_points: Reconcile headline demand with the cash needed to fulfill it.
Evaluate acquisition integration, regulatory delay and management distraction separately from strategic fit.
State limits of technical expertise while retaining conditional risks.
Distinguish useful AI applications from adequate aggregate returns on infrastructure spending.
tools_and_charts: Oracle RPO, earnings, capex, debt and share-price sequence
Toll Brothers backlog, EPS and revenue
Competing Warner Bros. bid structures and streaming market definition
transcript_cautions: Oracle periods are called third and fourth quarter in speech but the December report is fiscal Q2 2026.
The montage repeats the full discussion.
Sebastian is a viewer whose edited email Eisman reads; its detailed claims are not Eisman’s own measured findings.
AI researcher name is garbled; retained as attributed research commentary without guessing an identity.

claims.claim: Oracle’s AI backlog and revenues are growing rapidly, but its own operating cash generation cannot fund the associated buildout, increasing reliance on borrowing.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Reconcile capex, operating cash flow, borrowings and customer receipts each quarter.
claims.reason: The contemporaneous report shows six-month capex more than twice operating cash flow, negative trailing FCF, and higher borrowings. This directly validates the financing gap at the stated date, not future insolvency.

evidence.title: Fiscal 2026 second-quarter results
evidence.finding: RPO $523 billion, revenue $16.1 billion. Six-month operating cash flow $10.206 billion versus capex $20.535 billion. Trailing FCF negative $13.181 billion. Current/noncurrent borrowings $8.091/$99.984 billion, previously $7.271/$85.297 billion.

claims.next_check: Obtain primary evidence matching the stated metric, period and conditions before assigning an outcome grade.
